listing_view.reasoning: Subscription built to 12.15x by close on day three, with most of the demand arriving only on the final day (0.6x midday day two to 12.2x at close), which is typical QIB-led late demand rather than broad retail conviction. That supports a decent debut, but I have no grey market data, no anchor book, and no fresh-vs-OFS split, so this is a lean, not a conviction call.

longterm_view.reasoning: The earnings look strong — PAT roughly ₹4,100m against a ₹5131m raise, ~15-16% growth — but only about 31 paisa of every rupee of EBITDA arrived as cash in the latest year, down from ~49 paisa the year before, and borrowings jumped from ₹1,319m to ₹16,826m in two years to bridge the gap. An ARC's profits are inherently accounting estimates of recoveries on distressed assets bought years earlier; when profit-quality is this low and leverage is rising 13x, the reported growth is doing a lot of uncorroborated work. The document also prints a debt-to-equity of 0.39 where its own numbers give 0.546, which does not help trust in the tables.

governance.reasoning: Promoter shares are disclosed as partially pledged across all three years [promoters, page 273], and there is litigation flow from/against SBI involving cheque dishonour, forgery and fraud claims [litigation, page 436] — none damning on its own, but pledging plus an unreconciled leverage figure in the seller's own document warrants discount, not benefit of the doubt.

key_risks.risk: Profit is not converting to cash
key_risks.why_it_matters: Only ~0.31 of EBITDA and ~0.38 of PAT became operating cash in the latest year, so reported growth is heavily an accounting outcome, and the gap is being funded by debt.
Borrowings went from ₹1,319m to ₹16,826m in two years and the document itself flags refinancing risk that would raise financing costs and constrain future ability.
The document prints debt-to-equity at 0.39 where its own figures compute to 0.546; when the seller's arithmetic does not reconcile, every other derived figure deserves suspicion.
Partial pledging of promoter holdings is disclosed across FY2024-FY2026, creating forced-sale overhang if the stock corrects.

Criminal cases for cheque dishonour, forgery and fraud claims sit in the litigation chapter of a financial-sector seller's book; unresolved outcomes could impair reputation with exactly the banks an ARC must buy assets from.

answers.question: check receivables and inventory against the sales growth
answers.answer: Receivables are not the strain: receivable days are 59.3/44.1/46.7 — the latest year is only modestly worse than FY2024 and sales grew 26%, so invoiced collections are roughly keeping pace with sales. The real mismatch is not in the receivables line but in cash conversion: operating cash flow was ₹1,536m against PAT of ₹4,078m (only ~0.38 converts), meaning the profit is being recognised well before — and largely without — the cash, which is exactly what one expects from an ARC recognising estimated recoveries upfront. Inventory is not separately disclosed in what I was given and is unlikely to be meaningful for this business model. Net: sales growth looks real on billing terms but is only ~31-38% corroborated by cash.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that the latest year's low cash conversion is timing (e.g., a large acquisition of security receipts late in the year that has since started paying out) plus a reconciliation of the 0.39 vs 0.546 debt-to-equity discrepancy would move me materially higher; conversely, confirmation this is a pure offer for sale with exit-seeking promoters would move me lower.
